rules: Each player gets a bingo card and a pencil.
Walk slowly with a grown-up. When you see something on your card, point it out and say why it fits.
If the others agree, tick that square.
The first person to tick 4 squares in a row, across, down or corner to corner, shouts 'Bingo!'
Keep playing until everyone has a bingo, or the walk ends.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a bingo card and a pencil. 2. Read the squares aloud together before you leave.
flow.say: On this walk, we hunt for plants of every kind. When you spot one on your card, tell us why it fits.
flow.kid: Read your bingo card. Can you guess where you will find each one?
flow.context: This is the first step of Five Kinds Bingo, a game for a walk. You spot trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers.

flow.do: Walk slowly around your street, building or park, or look from the windows and balcony. Stop at each plant someone points out.
flow.say: What have you found? How do you know they're a climber and not a creeper?
flow.kid: Look high and low. Point at a plant. Say why they fit a square.
flow.parent: Stay with your child near roads. Do not touch plants with thorns or milky sap, and do not pick anything in someone else's garden.

flow.do: Stop at a plant with a stem that climbs or spreads.
flow.say: Look at this stem. Is it hard or soft? Is it standing, climbing or lying down?
flow.kid: Feel this stem gently. Is it hard or soft? Is it climbing or lying down?

check.q: A plant has a soft stem and lies along the ground over a big patch. What kind of plant is this?
check.why: A creeper has a weak stem that spreads along the ground. Picking 'shrub' often means thinking any low plant is a shrub. A shrub has hard, woody stems and stands up by itself.

flow.do: At home, look at the ticked squares together.
flow.say: Which square was hardest to find? Did you find a plant that did not fit any kind?
flow.kid: Which square was hardest? Did any plant break the rules?
flow.think: Was the plant growing out of a crack in the wall planted by anyone? How did they get there?

experiments.title: The Stem Test: which stems can stand up alone?
experiments.question: Which stems can hold themselves up, and how are they different from the ones that cannot?
experiments.predict: Before you test, line up the stems from the one you think is hardest to the softest. Which ones do you think will stand up by themselves, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, test every stem in the same three ways, in the same order. Use pieces of about the same length, as long as you can find (about 30 cm is good). Use stems from the kitchen or ones already cut or fallen, so no plant is hurt.
results_table: Bend test: springs back, snaps or flops?
Stand test: does it stand up alone?

materials.item: a woody stem: a twig fallen from a street tree, a neem datun stick from the market, or a pruned stem from an old tulsi or rose plant
two soft stems from the kitchen: a mint stem and a methi or coriander stem (the stalk the leaves grow on)
a money plant stem about 30 cm long, if you grow one or a neighbour can spare a cutting. Skip it if you have none
a hand lens, if you have one
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Use only stems from your kitchen, or pieces that have already fallen or been pruned. Do not use stems with milky sap or thorns. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Collect the stems. Do the nail, bend and stand tests. Fill in the table. Sort the stems into kinds.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for every stem. Then draw each stem and write woody or soft under it.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you test pieces of stem to find out which are woody and which are soft. The stem is the best clue to a plant's kind.

setup.art: Four stem pieces lined up on a sheet of newspaper: a brown twig, a mint stem, a methi stem and a long money plant stem.
setup.caption: 1. Line up your stems, hardest guess first.

setup.art: A child's thumbnail pressing gently into a green stalk, leaving a small dent.
setup.caption: 2. Nail test: press gently with a fingernail. Does it dent?

setup.art: Two hands bending a twig until it snaps, and a soft stalk flopping over.
setup.caption: 3. Bend test: does it spring back, snap or flop?

setup.art: A hand holding a stem upright by its bottom end. One stem stands straight, another droops.
setup.caption: 4. Stand test: hold the bottom end. Does it stand up alone?

flow.do: 1. Collect 4 or 5 stem pieces, from the kitchen or fallen from plants. 2. Lay them on newspaper. 3. Ask your child to line them up, hardest first, and say which will stand up alone.
flow.say: Which of these stems do you think is the hardest? Line them up, hardest first. Which ones will stand up by themselves? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Line up your stems, hardest first. Which will stand up alone? Why?

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: It feels hard like a stick.
It came from a big tree.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Stem Test. You find out which stems are woody and which are soft.

flow.do: 1. Pick up each stem. 2. Press a fingernail into it gently, near the middle. 3. Look closely, with the hand lens if you have one. 4. Write yes or no in the 'dent' column.
flow.say: Press your nail in gently. Does it leave a mark? A soft stem dents easily. A woody stem hardly dents at all.
flow.kid: Press your nail gently into each stem. Does it dent? Write yes or no.
flow.parent: Soft herb stems like mint dent easily and may feel juicy. Woody twigs barely mark.

flow.do: 1. Hold each stem at both ends. 2. Bend it gently into a curve, then let go. 3. Write what happened: springs back, snaps or flops.
flow.say: Now bend each one slowly. Does it spring back, snap, or flop over?
flow.kid: Bend each stem slowly. Does it spring back? Does it snap? Or does it flop?
flow.parent: A dry woody twig often snaps with a crack. A fresh green twig may spring back. A soft herb stem bends and stays bent, or flops. A money plant stem bends easily.

flow.do: 1. Hold each stem upright by its bottom end only. 2. See whether it stands straight or droops. 3. Fill in the stand column.
flow.say: Hold it from the bottom. Can it stand up straight by itself, or does it droop over?
flow.kid: Hold each stem at the bottom. Does it stand up by itself?

check.q: Suppose a long money plant stem flops over when you hold it up by its bottom end. At home, a money plant grows up a pole or a window grill. What kind of plant is a money plant?
check.why: A climber has a thin, bendy stem that cannot hold itself up. So they hold on to something and grow up it. A money plant grips with little roots on their stem. Picking 'herb' is a good guess, because the stem is green and soft. But a herb stays small and stands up alone. They do not climb.

flow.parent: Short pieces may stand even if they are soft, so use the longest pieces you have. A long stem has more weight to hold up. The woody twig stays stiff. A long money plant stem flops over.

flow.do: Look at the finished table together and fill in the last two columns.
flow.say: Look at the table. Which stems were woody? Which plants could they come from?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which stems are woody? Which are soft?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: woody stems can hold a plant up, and thin soft stems cannot. What I saw: the twig did not dent and stood up straight, but the money plant flopped over. Why: wood is hard, so a tree can stand alone. A money plant has to hold on to something to grow up.

experiments.title: Shade Detective: how much cooler is it under a tree?
experiments.question: How much cooler is the ground in the shade of a tree than in the sun?
experiments.predict: Before you measure, guess. Which place will be hottest: the sunny ground, the shade of a tree, or the shade of an umbrella? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, measure all the places at about the same time of day, on the same kind of ground, for example all on paving. Leave the thermometer for the same time in each place, 3 minutes.
results_table: My guess: hottest, middle or coolest

materials.item: a thermometer, a simple digital one is easiest
an umbrella
a timer or a phone clock
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Do this with a grown-up. Wear a cap. Do not stand in strong sun for long. Drink water. Keep away from traffic.

schedule.what: On a sunny day, about midday, measure the ground temperature in the sun, under a tree, under a shrub and under an umbrella. Make a bar chart.

experiments.record: Write the temperature for each place. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each place.
experiments.context: If there is a tree near your building, this experiment measures how much cooler the ground is in their shade than in the sun. A thermometer is a tool that measures how hot or cold something is.

setup.art: A digital thermometer lying on sunny paving stones in bright light.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the thermometer on sunny ground for 3 minutes. Read it.

setup.art: The same thermometer lying on the ground in the deep shade under a neem tree.
setup.caption: 2. Move it to the shade under a tree. Wait 3 minutes. Read it.

setup.art: The thermometer on the ground under an open umbrella, then under a hibiscus bush.
setup.caption: 3. Try the shade of an umbrella and of a shrub.

flow.do: 1. Choose a sunny time, near midday. 2. Find a spot in full sun, a big tree with thick shade, a shrub and a place for an umbrella. 3. Ask your child to guess which will be hottest and coolest.
flow.say: Which place do you think will be the hottest? Which will be the coolest? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which place will be hottest? Which will be coolest?
flow.context: This is the first step of Shade Detective. You measure how hot the ground is in the sun and in different shade.

flow.do: 1. Lay the thermometer on the sunny ground. 2. Wait 3 minutes. 3. Read it and write it down. 4. Do the same under the tree.
flow.say: We'll leave it 3 minutes in each place, so it has time to warm up or cool down. That keeps the test fair.
flow.kid: Put the thermometer on sunny ground. Wait 3 minutes. Read it. Then try under the tree.
flow.parent: Read the number together. Most digital thermometers show degrees Celsius. In summer, sunny paving can be more than 10 degrees hotter than deep shade.

flow.do: Measure under a shrub and under an open umbrella, 3 minutes each, the same way.
flow.say: Now let's try a shrub and an umbrella. Will they be as cool as the tree?
flow.kid: Now try under a shrub. Then under an umbrella. Write each number.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart, one bar for each place.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. The taller the bar, the hotter the place.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each place. Taller bar means hotter.

chart.title: Made-up example results: ground temperature at midday
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: In the Shade Detective test, why might the ground under a big tree be cooler than under an umbrella?
options: The tree's leaves block sunlight, and the tree also gives off water that cools the air
The tree's trunk is cold inside
check.why: Both the umbrella and the leaves block sunlight. A tree also lets water evaporate from their leaves, and that takes heat away, like sweat on your skin. A big tree's shade is also wider and thicker. Picking 'the umbrella makes heat' is a natural guess, because an umbrella feels warm. It gets warm because it soaks up sunlight, but it does not make heat of its own.

flow.do: Ask your child for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you measure? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I measured. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a big tree gives the coolest shade. What I saw: the sun was 46 degrees and the tree shade was 31 degrees. Why: the leaves stop the sunlight, and the tree gives off water that cools the air.

experiments.title: The Smell Test: which leaves are the strongest?
experiments.question: Which kitchen leaves have the strongest smell, and why do plants make smells at all?
experiments.predict: Before you sniff, guess. Line up the leaves, strongest smell first. Why do you think that one will smell strongest?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use one leaf of each, about the same size. Crush each the same way, between your fingers, for 5 seconds. Each person scores every leaf from 0 (no smell) to 5 (very strong).
results_table: Person 3 score (if a third person smells)

materials.item: one leaf each of 5 kitchen plants: for example mint, coriander, curry leaf, methi and spinach, and tulsi if you grow them
a small plate or paper square for each leaf, numbered

experiments.safety: Smell only. Never taste the leaves. Use only plants a grown-up knows are safe, like kitchen herbs. Do not use kaner, datura or any unknown plant. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Crush and smell 5 leaves. Score them. Find the middle score. Talk about why plants make smells.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then circle the leaf with the strongest smell.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you crush and smell leaves to find out which have the strongest smell. Strong smells are often a plant's way of keeping safe.

setup.art: Five numbered plates, each with one leaf: mint, coriander, curry leaf, methi and spinach.
setup.caption: 1. Put one leaf on each numbered plate.

setup.art: A child's fingers rubbing a mint leaf, with little curly smell lines rising from it.
setup.caption: 2. Crush a leaf between your fingers for 5 seconds.

setup.art: The child sniffing the crushed leaf, then holding up four fingers to give a score.
setup.caption: 3. Sniff and give it a score from 0 to 5.

flow.do: 1. Put one leaf on each numbered plate. 2. Ask your child to guess which smells strongest, and line them up.
flow.say: Which leaf do you think has the strongest smell? Let's line them up from strongest to weakest.
flow.kid: Look at the leaves. Which will smell strongest? Line them up.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Smell Test. You crush leaves and score their smell from 0 to 5.

flow.do: 1. Crush leaf 1 between your fingers for 5 seconds. 2. Each person sniffs it and gives a score from 0 to 5. 3. Rest your nose for a moment, or sniff your own sleeve. 4. Wipe your fingers and do the next leaf.
flow.say: Crush it for five seconds. Now sniff. Give it a score. Zero means no smell. Five means very strong.
flow.kid: Crush the leaf for five seconds. Sniff. Score it from 0 to 5.
flow.parent: Noses get tired quickly. A short rest, or sniffing your own sleeve, between leaves helps. Do not let anyone taste the leaves.

flow.do: Find the middle score for each leaf. With three scores, put them in order and take the middle one. With only two people, add the two scores instead and compare the totals.
flow.say: Each of us scored differently. To be fair, we take the middle score, or add our scores if there are two of us.
flow.kid: Put the three scores in order. The middle one is the middle score. With two people, add your scores.

chart.title: Made-up example results: middle smell scores
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your family's noses will give different scores.

flow.do: Talk about why plants make smells.
flow.say: Plants can't run away from insects. Many make strong smelly chemicals in their leaves. Insects often don't like them. Some of these same chemicals are what we use as spices and medicines.
flow.kid: Plants cannot run away. So some make strong smells. Many insects dislike them. People use these smells in food and medicine.

check.q: In the Smell Test, mint had a strong smell when crushed. What is the most likely reason a plant makes a strong smell?
options: To protect themselves from insects and animals that eat leaves
check.why: Strong-smelling chemicals in leaves often keep away insects and animals that would eat the plant. People found these chemicals useful later, as spices and medicines. Picking 'to make people happy' is a kind thought, but plants made these smells long before there were any people.

flow.do: Ask your child for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you smell? Why do you think some leaves smell so strong?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I smelled. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: mint and curry leaf have the strongest smell. What I saw: they scored 5 and 4, and spinach scored 1. Why: these plants make smelly chemicals in their leaves that keep many insects away. People use the same chemicals in food.

activities.title: Plant Count: the five-kinds survey

materials.item: a clipboard or notebook with the tally table
a pencil

activities.safety: If you go outside, go only with a grown-up. Do not touch plants with thorns or milky sap.

schedule.what: Look from every window and the balcony, and walk to your building gate if you can. Make a tally mark for every plant of each kind. Count the tallies.

activities.record: A tally table with five rows: tree, shrub, herb, climber, creeper. Add one plant name you know for each kind.
activities.context: This is a short survey of the plants around your home. You count how many trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers you can see.

setup.art: A notebook page with a tally table of five rows, each row with a small picture: tree, bush, small plant, climbing vine, spreading vine.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a tally table with five kinds.

setup.art: A child at a balcony grill pointing at a money plant climbing it, with a tree visible across the road.
setup.caption: 2. Look from each window and the balcony. Decide each plant's kind.

setup.art: The tally table filled with groups of four lines crossed by a fifth.
setup.caption: 3. Make a tally mark for each plant. Count them at the end.

flow.do: Show your child the tally table, and explain the five kinds in one line each.
flow.say: Let's count plants. For each plant, we decide: tree, shrub, herb, climber or creeper. Then we make a tally mark.
flow.kid: Count the plants you can see. Decide each one's kind. Make a tally mark.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Plant Count. You count plants of each kind around your home.

flow.do: Stop at the first plant you can see clearly, in a pot or from a window. Look at their stem together.
flow.say: What do you notice about this plant? What do you wonder about them?
flow.kid: Look at this plant. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

ask.q: What do you notice about their stem?
good: It is holding on to the wall.

flow.do: For about 12 minutes, look from every window and the balcony. Look at pots at home too, and walk to your building gate if you can. At each plant, your child decides the kind and makes a tally mark.
flow.say: Look high and low. Look at walls, grills and cracks too. What kind is this one?
flow.kid: Look up and look down. Make a tally mark for each plant.
flow.parent: Do not worry about being exactly right. The point is to look at stems. If you both disagree, write it in a 'not sure' row. That is honest science.

flow.do: Count each row of tallies together.
flow.say: Which kind did we see most? Which did we see least? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Count each row. Which kind did you see most? Which least?

check.q: Meera, a girl in Class 3, sees a plant with a thin stem growing up her window grill. This plant has little roots along their stem. What kind of plant is this?
check.why: A climber has a thin stem and holds on to something to grow up. A money plant does this with little roots. Picking 'creeper' means mixing up the two thin-stemmed kinds. A creeper spreads along the ground instead of going up.

flow.think: Which plants did someone plant on purpose? Which grew by themselves?

activities.title: The Plant Hunt at Home

materials.item: a sheet of paper divided into six boxes: food, medicine, wood, cloth and rope, shade and other
a pencil

activities.safety: Look at medicines and kitchen things, but do not open, eat or taste anything.

schedule.what: Hunt for 10 minutes. Write or draw each thing that came from a plant in the right box. Count them.

activities.record: The six-box sheet, with at least 20 things that came from plants.
activities.context: In this hunt, you find everything in your home that came from a plant, and sort the things by how we use them.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with six boxes, each with a picture: a plate, a medicine bottle, a chair, a T-shirt, a tree's shade and a question mark.
setup.caption: 1. Make a sheet with six boxes for six uses.

setup.art: A child opening a kitchen cupboard full of dal, rice, spices and tea, with a pencil behind one ear.
setup.caption: 2. Hunt in the kitchen, cupboards and rooms.

setup.art: A child drawing a jute bag in the 'cloth and rope' box, with an arrow back to a tall jute plant.
setup.caption: 3. Draw or write each thing in its box.

flow.do: Give your child the six-box sheet and a pencil.
flow.say: How many things in our home came from a plant? Let's hunt. You have ten minutes.
flow.kid: Find everything in your home that came from a plant. You have ten minutes. Go!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Plant Hunt at Home. You find things that came from plants and sort them by use.

flow.do: Let your child hunt. Help with tricky ones: paper, rubber chappals, cotton clothes, a wooden spoon, coconut oil, tea, sugar, turmeric, a jute bag.
flow.say: Look everywhere: the kitchen, the cupboard, your clothes, your school bag. Where does each thing really come from?
flow.kid: Look in the kitchen. Look at your clothes and your books. Where did each thing come from?
flow.parent: Surprising ones: paper is made from wood, and sugar comes from a grass called sugarcane. Natural rubber comes from a tree's milky sap. Milk and eggs count too, because cows and hens eat plants.

flow.do: Count the things in each box together.
flow.say: Which box has the most things in it? Is there any box that is empty?
flow.kid: Count each box. Which box is the fullest?

check.q: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, has chappals made of natural rubber. Where does natural rubber come from?
options: From a rock dug out of the ground
From the milky sap of a rubber tree
check.why: Natural rubber is made from a milky sap, called latex, that comes out when the bark of a rubber tree is cut. In India, many rubber trees grow in Kerala. Many chappals today use rubber made in factories from oil, but natural rubber comes from trees.

flow.do: Imagine a breakfast with no plants at all.
flow.say: If every plant disappeared, what would be left for breakfast? Think about milk and eggs too.
flow.kid: Imagine there are no plants. What could you eat for breakfast?
flow.think: Is there any food at all that does not come from a plant in the end?

activities.title: Hug a Tree: how big are they, and how old?

materials.item: a long piece of string, at least 3 metres
a measuring tape or a 30 cm ruler
crayons and thin paper for a bark rubbing

activities.safety: Choose a tree in a safe place, away from traffic. Check for ants, thorns and wasps before you hug.

schedule.what: Hug the tree. Measure around their trunk with string. Make a bark rubbing. Estimate their age.

activities.record: Write the distance around the trunk in centimetres. Write your estimate of the tree's age. Stick the bark rubbing next to it.
activities.context: In this activity, you measure around a tree trunk with string, and use a rough rule to guess how old the tree is.

setup.art: A child hugging a tree trunk, arms not reaching all the way around, a parent smiling.
setup.caption: 1. Hug the tree. Can your arms reach round?

setup.art: A string wrapped around a tree trunk at the height of a grown-up's chest, with a finger pinching the place where the ends meet.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap string round the trunk at a grown-up's chest height.

setup.art: The string laid straight along a measuring tape on the ground.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the string along a tape and read the length.

setup.art: Thin paper held on bark while a crayon rubs over it, showing the bark's pattern.
setup.caption: 4. Make a bark rubbing with a crayon.

flow.do: Choose a big tree nearby and let your child hug them.
flow.say: Let's hug this tree. Can your arms reach all the way round? How many of us would we need?
flow.kid: Hug the tree. Can your arms meet? How many people would it take?
flow.context: This is the first step of Hug a Tree. You measure around a trunk and guess the tree's age.

flow.do: 1. Wrap the string around the trunk at about a grown-up's chest height. 2. Pinch the string where it meets. 3. Lay it along the tape and read the length in centimetres.
flow.say: We measure at chest height, because that's how foresters do it everywhere. That way everyone's measurements can be compared.
flow.kid: Wrap the string round the trunk. Pinch where it meets. Measure the string.

flow.do: Use the rough rule: many trees grow about 2 and a half centimetres around each year. Divide the distance around by 2 and a half.
flow.say: Here's a rough rule foresters use. Many trees get about 2 and a half centimetres fatter around, each year. So we divide.
flow.kid: Many trees grow about 2 and a half centimetres round each year. So divide to guess the age.
flow.parent: This is a rough rule of thumb. Trees grow at very different speeds: a fast teak and a slow tamarind can be very different. So the answer is a rough guess, not a fact. Say so to your child. For example, 150 cm divided by 2.5 is 60, so about 60 years old.

check.q: In Hug a Tree, a trunk measured 100 cm around. Using the rough rule of 2 and a half cm a year, about how old is the tree?
check.why: 100 divided by 2 and a half is 40. You can check: 40 times 2 and a half is 100. So the tree is roughly 40 years old. Picking 10 often means dividing by 10 instead. Picking 250 means multiplying instead of dividing. Remember this is only a rough guess, because trees grow at different speeds.

flow.do: Hold thin paper against the bark and rub the side of a crayon over it.
flow.say: Bark protects the tree, like our skin. Every kind of tree has its own bark pattern. Let's collect this tree's pattern.
flow.kid: Hold paper on the bark. Rub a crayon over it. Look at the pattern!
flow.think: Why do you think a tree needs bark? What would happen without it?

activities.title: The Banana Plant Puzzle: tree or giant herb?

materials.item: a piece of banana stem, about 15 cm long, sold as vazhaithandu or kele ka tana in many markets, especially in south India. Buy it fresh on the day
a kitchen knife and a chopping board, used only by a grown-up
a twig from any tree, for comparing

activities.safety: Only a grown-up uses the knife. Banana stem sap can stain clothes, so wear old clothes or an apron.

schedule.what: Cut a banana stem across. Peel its layers. Compare it with a tree twig. Decide: tree or herb?

activities.record: Draw the cut end of the banana stem and the cut end of the twig, side by side. Write which one has wood.
activities.context: A banana plant looks like a tree. In this activity, you cut open a banana stem from the market to see whether it has any wood inside.

setup.art: A pale green banana stem piece on a chopping board, with a grown-up's hand holding a knife ready to cut across it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the banana stem straight across.

setup.art: The cut end of the banana stem showing rings of rolled layers, like an onion, with a child's finger peeling one away.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the cut end. Peel off one layer.

setup.art: The cut end of a brown twig next to the banana stem, showing solid wood in the twig.
setup.caption: 3. Compare it with the cut end of a tree twig.

flow.do: Show your child the banana stem piece, still whole.
flow.say: This comes from a banana plant. People call them a banana tree. Are they really a tree? What do you think we'll find inside?
flow.kid: This is part of a banana plant's trunk. Is a banana plant a tree? Guess what is inside.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Banana Plant Puzzle. You cut open a banana stem to see if a banana plant is really a tree.

flow.do: Cut the stem straight across, on the board. Let your child look closely at the cut end.
flow.say: Look at the cut end. What do you see? Is it hard, like wood?
flow.kid: Your grown-up cuts it. Look at the cut end. What do you see?
flow.parent: You will see layers, rolled one inside another like an onion, often with threads and juicy, spongy tissue. There is no wood.

flow.do: Let your child peel off one or two layers with their fingers.
flow.say: Each layer is the bottom of a leaf. The leaves grow from the middle and wrap around each other. That's what makes the 'trunk'.
flow.kid: Peel off one layer. It is the bottom of a leaf. The trunk is rolled-up leaves!

check.q: In the Banana Plant Puzzle, the stem was made of soft rolled layers with no wood. So what kind of plant is a banana?
options: A tree, because they are tall
A giant herb, because their stem is soft and not woody
check.why: A herb is any plant whose stem does not become wood. The banana's 'trunk' is made of rolled-up leaf bottoms, so botanists call them a giant herb, even though they are tall. Picking 'tree' means sorting by size. The real clue is what the stem is made of.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the tree twig across. Compare the two ends.
flow.say: Now look at the twig. Can you peel it? What is different?
flow.kid: Look at the twig's cut end. Can you peel it? What is different?
flow.think: What other plants look like trees, but might not be?

flow.do: Optional: a grown-up cooks the banana stem, if your family eats it. It is used in curries and juice in many Indian homes.
flow.say: Many families in south India cook banana stem. The banana plant gives us fruit, leaves for plates, stem for food and fibre for rope.
flow.kid: Banana plants give fruit, leaf plates, food and rope. Which use is most surprising?
flow.parent: Banana leaves are used as plates, and banana fibre is made into rope, mats and even cloth.

activities.title: The Circling Shoot: watch a climber search

materials.item: a young climber in a pot, like a bean or bottle gourd seedling about two weeks old, with a free shoot tip (sow the seeds two weeks before)
a stick or pencil pushed into the soil next to them
a phone camera, or paper and pencil

schedule.what: Take a photo of the shoot tip from above every 30 minutes for 2 to 3 hours, or mark its position on paper.
Look at the photos in order. Has the tip moved in a circle? Has it found the stick? Talk about how a climber differs from a tree.

activities.record: Draw a dot for each position of the tip, from above, and join the dots.
activities.context: Climbers search for something to hold. In this activity, you take photos of a climbing shoot over a few hours to see it moving.

setup.art: A young bean plant in a pot on a windowsill, their shoot tip waving in the air, with a pencil standing in the soil nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Put a stick in the pot near a young climber.

setup.art: A phone held directly above the pot, taking a photo of the shoot tip.
setup.caption: 2. Every 30 minutes, photograph the tip from above.

setup.art: A paper with dots joined in a looping circle around a centre point.
setup.caption: 3. Mark each position and join the dots.

flow.do: Choose a young climber with a shoot tip waving in the air. Push a stick into the soil about a finger-length away from the stem.
flow.say: This climber needs something to hold. Will they find this stick? Let's watch them, like a slow-motion film.
flow.kid: Put a stick near the climber. Will the climber find it?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Circling Shoot. You watch a climbing plant's tip move over a few hours.

flow.do: Photograph the shoot tip from directly above every 30 minutes for 2 to 3 hours. Keep the phone in the same place each time.
flow.say: We take the photo from the same place every time. That way we can compare them fairly.
flow.kid: Take a photo from above every 30 minutes. Stand in the same place.
flow.parent: If you have no phone, put a paper under the pot and mark where the tip is above it with a dot. Charles Darwin timed climbing shoots like this. A hop shoot took about two hours to swing round once.

flow.do: On Day 2, look at the photos in order, or join the dots on the paper.
flow.say: Look at the dots. Is the tip moving in a line, or in a circle? Has it touched the stick yet?
flow.kid: Look at your photos in order. Did the tip move? Which way?

check.q: In the Circling Shoot, the tip of a climbing bean moved slowly in a loop. Why do climbers do this?
options: To sweep around and find something to hold on to
The wind blows them in circles
check.why: A climber's shoot tip moves slowly in loops, sweeping the space around it, until it touches a support. Then it wraps around it and climbs. Picking 'the wind' is a good idea to test. If you keep the pot indoors with no breeze and it still circles, the movement comes from the plant.

flow.parent: In 2 to 3 hours the tip may not reach the stick yet. That is fine: you are looking for the slow loop, not for the grip.

flow.do: Talk about how a climber is different from a tree.
flow.say: A tree builds a trunk. A climber searches for a support instead. Which do you think is quicker?
flow.kid: A tree builds a trunk. A climber searches for help. Which is faster?
flow.think: If the climber never finds a stick, what do you think they will do?

activities.title: Twist a Plant Rope

materials.item: jute twine, or coir from a coconut husk or a coir scrubber, or long dry grass
a small bag and some coins, to test the rope

schedule.what: Pull out some plant fibres. Twist them into a two-strand rope. Test how much it can hold.

activities.record: Tape a piece of your rope here. Write how many coins it held, and how many the loose bunch held.
activities.context: People have made rope from plants for thousands of years. In this activity, you twist plant fibres into a rope of your own.

setup.art: Loose brown fibres pulled from a piece of jute twine, spread on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Pull out a bunch of long fibres.

setup.art: Two hands twisting a bunch of fibres tightly in one direction.
setup.caption: 2. Twist the bunch tightly in one direction.

setup.art: The twisted bunch folded in half so it coils around itself into a two-strand rope.
setup.caption: 3. Fold it in half and let it twist around itself into a rope.

flow.do: Pull out a bunch of long fibres, about as long as your arm.
flow.say: Jute and coir come from plants. Jute comes from the stem of the jute plant. Coir comes from the hairy husk of a coconut.
flow.kid: Pull out some long fibres. They came from a plant!
flow.context: This is the first step of Twist a Plant Rope. You make rope from plant fibres, the way people have for thousands of years.

flow.do: 1. Hold one end of the bunch, or tie it to a door handle. 2. Twist the other end tightly in one direction, until it starts to kink. 3. Fold it in half, holding both ends. 4. Let go of the middle. It twists around itself into a rope. 5. Tie a knot at the end.
flow.say: Twist, twist, twist. Now fold it in half and watch. The twisted bunch springs back, and the only way it can untwist is by wrapping round itself.
flow.kid: Twist the fibres tight. Fold them in half. Watch them wrap into a rope!

flow.do: 1. Make a second bunch the same size, but do not twist it. 2. Hang a small bag from each, tied on the same way, and add coins one at a time until it pulls apart. 3. Test the loose bunch first, then your rope.
flow.say: Let's test it. How many coins does the loose bunch hold? How many does our rope hold?
flow.kid: Hang a bag of coins from the loose bunch. Then from your rope. Which holds more?

check.q: In Twist a Plant Rope, why did the twisted rope hold more coins than the loose fibres?
options: Twisting makes the fibres grip each other, so they all share the pull
The coins were lighter the second time
check.why: When fibres are twisted, they press and grip each other. So a pull on the rope is shared by all of them at once. Loose fibres slide apart and break one by one. Picking 'heavier' often means thinking strong things must be heavy. The rope weighs the same as the fibres it was made from.

flow.do: Look for plant ropes and fibres at home: a jute bag, a coir doormat, a cotton string, a rope cot.
flow.say: Ropes for boats, cots and wells were made from plants like coir, jute and hemp for thousands of years.
flow.kid: Find something at home made from plant fibre.
flow.think: Why do you think coir ropes are used on boats in Kerala?

projects.title: My Plant Friend: a 4-week diary

materials.item: a notebook to be the plant diary
a piece of string and a measuring tape or ruler
crayons

schedule.what: Choose a plant friend. Decide their kind. Draw them, give them a name and make a bark or leaf rubbing.
Visit your plant. Count new leaves, buds or flowers. Note any visitors: ants, birds, bees, butterflies.
Visit again. Measure something: the length of one new shoot, or around the trunk. Find out one way people use this kind of plant.
Visit again. Draw them from the same spot as Day 1. What has changed?
Last visit. Write a 'plant friend card' with their kind, their uses, their visitors and what changed.

projects.record: A 4-week plant diary with 5 drawings, a rubbing, measurements, a list of visitors and a plant friend card.
projects.context: In this 4-week project, you make friends with one plant near your home. You visit them every week and keep a diary about them.

setup.art: A child sitting on a step drawing a curry leaf shrub in a notebook, with a name tag tied loosely to a branch.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a plant friend. Draw them and give them a name.

setup.art: A child counting tiny new leaves on the same shrub, a bee nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Each week, count new leaves, flowers and visitors.

check.q: Your plant friend is a curry leaf shrub. What are they mostly used for?

challenges.title: A Ladder for a Climber
challenges.problem: A young bottle gourd or bean climber in a pot has nothing to climb. Their stem is flopping on the floor. Build them a support so they can climb up to the light, using only things from home.
constraints: Use only things you find at home.
The support must stand up by itself in the pot or next to it.
It must be at least 1 metre tall.
It must not hurt the plant.
materials: a young climber in a pot (sow bean seeds two weeks earlier, or use the climber from the Circling Shoot)
sticks, bamboo skewers, old pens, string, wool, a coat hanger, an old dupatta, newspaper rolls
general: Push one long stick into the soil, and gently twist the climber around it.
Make a teepee: tie three sticks together at the top, like a tent.
Tie strings from the pot up to a window grill or a hook.
creative: Weave a net of string between two sticks, so tendrils have many places to grab.
Use a ladder shape made from skewers and string, so the climber can go up step by step.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own support. Draw it, build it, and check your climber every two days. Which way do they climb? Do they like your ladder?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a support for a climber, a plant that cannot stand up alone and needs something to hold.

setup.art: A bottle gourd seedling in a pot with their stem flopping onto the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the climber with nothing to hold.

setup.art: Three sticks tied together at the top like a small tent, pushed into a pot.
setup.caption: 2. Build a support, like a stick teepee.

setup.art: The same climber a week later, their tendrils curled around the sticks, reaching upward.
setup.caption: 3. Check every two days. Are they climbing?

flow.do: Look at the floppy climber together.
flow.say: This plant is a climber. Their stem is too thin to stand up. What do they need from us?
flow.kid: Look at this climber. Why are they flopping? What do they need?
flow.context: This is the first step of A Ladder for a Climber. You design a support for a climbing plant.

flow.do: Let your child draw two or three ideas for a support before building anything.
flow.say: Draw a few ideas first. Think: how will the plant hold on? With tendrils, or by twisting their stem?
flow.kid: Draw two ideas. How will the plant hold on to them?

check.q: A bottle gourd climbs with curly tendrils. Which support will they find easiest to hold?
options: A flat wall with nothing on it
check.why: Tendrils are thin and curl around thin things, like strings or wire. They cannot wrap around a thick, smooth pipe. Picking 'a wall' would suit a climber with little sticky roots, like money plant. Different climbers need different ladders.

flow.do: Build the support and gently guide the climber's tip onto it. Do not tie them tightly.
flow.say: Let's guide the tip gently onto the support. The plant will do the rest.
flow.kid: Build your support. Gently put the climber's tip on it.
flow.parent: If you tie the stem, use soft wool in a loose loop, so the stem can grow fatter.

flow.do: Check every two days for a week. Mark how high the climber has reached.
flow.say: How high have they climbed? Which way do they twist?
flow.kid: Check every two days. How high did they climb?

challenges.title: Cool the Hot Wall
challenges.problem: One wall of a house gets the afternoon sun, and the room behind it gets very hot. Plan a planting that will shade the wall. You must choose which kinds of plants to use, and where.
constraints: There is only a narrow strip of soil, about one hand-width wide, along the wall.
The plan must give shade within one year.
You can show it as a drawing or a cardboard model.
materials: paper and coloured pencils, or a cardboard box as the house
green paper or real leaves for the model
general: Plant a fast climber, like a gourd or a jasmine, and give them strings to climb up the wall.
Put pots of shrubs, like hibiscus, on the ground in front of the wall.
Plant a tree a little way out, for shade in later years.
creative: Grow a climber over a frame a little away from the wall, so air can flow behind the leaves and keep the wall cooler.
Choose a climber that also gives food, like bitter gourd, so the shade feeds the family too.
Mix a fast climber for this year with a slow tree for the future.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own plan. Which kinds of plants did you choose? Why? Use what you learned in Shade Detective about shade to explain your choices.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You plan which kinds of plants to grow to shade a hot wall: trees, shrubs or climbers.

setup.art: A house wall glowing orange in the afternoon sun, with a thin strip of soil at its foot.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the hot wall and the narrow strip of soil.

setup.art: A drawing of the same wall with a climber growing up strings and a shrub at the corner.
setup.caption: 2. Draw where each plant will go.

setup.art: A cardboard model house with green paper leaves on strings up one wall.
setup.caption: 3. Build a model of your plan.

flow.do: Find a hot wall at home or in your building. In the afternoon, touch it briefly with the back of your hand.
flow.say: Feel this wall. It's soaked up the sun all afternoon. How could plants help?
flow.kid: Feel the hot wall. How could plants make it cooler?
flow.context: This is the first step of Cool the Hot Wall. You plan which plants to grow to shade a hot wall.

flow.do: Talk through the kinds of plants and which would fit a narrow strip of soil.
flow.say: A tree needs lots of space and years to grow. A shrub is quicker. A climber needs only a little soil, and they can cover a whole wall.
flow.kid: Which kind fits a tiny strip of soil? Which grows fastest?

check.q: Which kind of plant can shade a whole wall from a strip of soil one hand-width wide?
check.why: A climber needs only a little soil for their roots, but their thin stem can climb high and spread leaves over the whole wall. Picking 'tree' makes sense for shade, but a tree needs much more room for their roots and many years to grow. A creeper spreads on the ground, not up the wall.

flow.do: Draw the plan or build the cardboard model.
flow.say: Show me where each plant goes. How will the climber get up the wall?
flow.kid: Draw your plan. Show each plant and how the climber goes up.

flow.do: Present the plan to the family.
flow.say: Tell us your plan. Why did you choose these kinds of plants?
flow.kid: Tell your family your plan. Say why you chose each plant.
flow.think: Could your plan help birds and bees too?

items.p: Sort these plants into their kinds.
items.a: as given
items.why: Trees have one woody trunk. Shrubs have many woody stems. Herbs have soft stems. Climbers hold on to grow up. Creepers spread on the ground.

items.p: Which plant is a shrub?
items.why: Hibiscus has several woody stems from near the ground, so hibiscus is a shrub. Mango is a tree, pumpkin is a creeper and coriander is a herb. Picking 'mango' often means choosing any plant with flowers or fruit.

items.p: In the Stem Test, a stem dented easily under your fingernail and bent over when you held it up. What kind of plant did it most likely come from?
items.why: A soft stem that dents and flops has no wood in it, so the plant is most likely a herb. Trees and shrubs have woody stems that hardly dent.
items.context: In the Stem Test, you pressed, bent and held up pieces of stem to find out which were woody.

items.p: All tall plants are trees.
items.why: False. Bamboo grows as tall as a house, but bamboo is a grass. A banana plant is tall too, but they have no wood, so they are a giant herb.

items.p: A plant with a thin stem that spreads along the ground is called a ____.
items.why: Pumpkin, watermelon and sweet potato are creepers. They spread over the ground.

items.p: Match each climber to how they hold on.
pairs: twisting their stem round a stick
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Climbers hold on in different ways: tendrils, little roots, twisting stems or thorns.

items.p: Why does a pumpkin grow along the ground instead of standing up?
opts: Their stem is too thin and weak to hold them up
They are afraid of the sun
They are a tree that fell over
items.why: A pumpkin's stem is long and soft, and their fruits are heavy. Lying on the ground, the stem does not have to hold them up. Picking 'a tree that fell' means thinking every plant wants to be a tree.

items.p: Match each thing to the plant that gave it.
pairs: a tree like teak or sal
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every one of these everyday things began as part of a plant.

items.p: Look at a plant near you. Are they a tree, shrub, herb, climber or creeper? Write how you know.
items.a: Any honest answer with a reason about the stem. For example, they are a shrub, because they have many hard, woody stems coming up from the soil.
items.why: The best clue is the stem: hard or soft, one or many, standing up, climbing or spreading.

items.p: Draw one tree, one shrub and one herb. Show how their stems are different.
items.a: A tree with one thick trunk, a shrub with many woody stems from the ground, and a small herb with a soft green stem.
items.why: The stem is the main way to tell these three kinds apart.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 3, says, 'A rose is a tree, because their stems are woody.' What has Nila got right, and what is her mistake?
items.a: Nila is right that a rose has woody stems. But a tree has one thick trunk. A rose has many woody stems coming up from near the ground, and stays small. So a rose is a shrub.
items.why: A strong answer uses two clues, not one: how hard the stem is, and how many main stems there are. Woody alone does not make a tree.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Coriander, spinach, mint, guava.
items.a: Guava, because a guava is a tree with one woody trunk. Coriander, spinach and mint are herbs with soft green stems.
items.why: The stem is the clue. Press a coriander or mint stem and they dent and bend. A guava trunk is hard wood.

items.p: A family in a Chennai flat has room for one pot on their sunny balcony. They are deciding what to grow.

views.says: A curry leaf shrub. We use curry leaves in our cooking every single day.
A tulsi herb. Tulsi grows quickly in a small pot, and we use the leaves when someone has a cough.
A money plant. They will climb up the balcony grill and shade our hot window.

items.ask: Which plant would you choose? Give a reason that uses the kind of plant they are and how people use them. Then say one good point another person made.
items.a: A strong answer links the choice to the plant's kind. A curry leaf shrub has woody stems and grows big, so they need a deep pot, but they give leaves for years. A tulsi is a herb. They grow fast in a small pot, and people use their leaves as a home remedy. A money plant is a climber, so they need the grill as a support, and they can shade a window. A strong answer then admits another person's good point.
items.why: Each choice is sensible. They trade off food, medicine, shade and space. What matters is using the plant's kind to say how they will grow in one small pot.

items.p: Which of these is NOT a way people use plants?
items.why: Iron is a metal dug from rocks. Food, medicine and shade all come from plants. Picking 'shade' often means forgetting that shade is a use too. People plant trees on purpose to cool their streets.

items.p: A shrub is just a baby tree that has not grown up yet.
items.why: False. A hibiscus or a rose stays a shrub all their life. They keep many woody stems from near the ground and never grow one big trunk. A young mango tree is small, but they already have one main stem.

items.p: A plant that holds on to a wall or a stick to grow upward is called a ____.
items.why: Money plant, pepper and bitter gourd are climbers.

items.p: In the story 'The Pepper Tree That Wasn't', why did the painter think pepper grew on a jackfruit tree?
opts: The pepper climber was holding on to the jackfruit trunk, so they looked like one plant
Jackfruit trees really do make pepper
Someone tied pepper on the tree
items.why: Pepper is a climber. They grow up a tree, holding on with little roots. From a distance, the two plants look like one. Picking 'jackfruit trees make pepper' is exactly the painter's mistake.
items.context: This question is about the story 'The Pepper Tree That Wasn't', about a Dutch painter in Kerala in 1675.

items.p: Tara, a girl in Class 4, puts a thermometer on the ground in three places at noon: in the sun, under an umbrella and under a neem tree. Predict which place will be coolest, and explain why.
items.a: Under the neem tree will be coolest. The umbrella and the tree both block the sunlight. But the tree's leaves also let out water, and water turning into vapour takes heat away. So the air under the tree is cooled twice over.
items.why: A strong answer says both block the Sun, and then gives the extra reason for the tree: water evaporating from the leaves cools them and the air around them.
items.context: In Shade Detective, you measure how hot the ground is in the sun and in shade with a thermometer.

items.p: A watermelon plant creeps over the hot sand of a riverbank. Their big leaves lie spread out on the ground. How might creeping help them there? What danger does it bring?
items.a: Creeping helps because the plant does not spend food on a stem strong enough to stand up. They can spread fast over the open sand and catch lots of sunlight. Their leaves also shade the sand, which keeps it a little damp. The danger is that animals and people can step on them or eat them, and taller plants nearby can shade them.
items.why: A strong answer gives a good point and a bad point. Every way of growing has a cost as well as a gain.

items.p: Rice, wheat and ragi are all herbs. Why do farmers grow herbs, not trees, to get grain?
opts: A herb grows from seed to grain in a few months, so a field gives a crop every season
items.why: A herb does not spend years building a woody trunk. They put their food into seeds quickly, often within four months. So farmers can sow and harvest again and again. Picking 'trees cannot make seeds' is wrong: mango and tamarind trees make plenty of seeds, but only after many years.

items.p: What does the word 'weed' really mean?
opts: A special poisonous kind of plant
A plant growing where people do not want it
items.why: 'Weed' is a word about our wishes. The same grass can be a weed in a vegetable patch and a lawn on a cricket field. Picking 'poisonous' often comes from hearing weeds called bad plants.

items.p: Why do some plants, like mint and tulsi, have strong smells?
opts: To protect themselves from insects and animals that eat leaves
items.why: Many plants make strong-smelling chemicals that keep leaf-eaters away. People use these same chemicals as spices and medicines.
items.context: In the Smell Test, you crushed leaves and scored how strong their smell was.

items.p: Teak wood is used for doors. Coriander is used for chutney. Why do we take wood from trees, but never from herbs?
items.a: A tree builds a hard, woody trunk, year after year. A herb's stem stays soft and green, with very little wood in it. So there is no wood in a coriander plant to make a door from.
items.why: A strong answer links the use to the kind of stem. The kind of plant tells us what we can use them for.

items.p: Put these in order, from the plant that gives the most shade to the least: a big banyan tree, a rose shrub, a coriander herb.
items.why: The bigger the plant and the more leaves high above you, the more shade they give.

items.p: Name three things in your home that came from plants. Say which plant, and which part of the plant, if you know.
items.a: Any three good answers. For example: my cotton shirt came from the fluffy seed hairs of the cotton plant. Paper came from wood. Rice came from the seeds of a grass.
items.why: Plants give us food, cloth, wood, paper, rubber, oil, colours and medicine.

items.p: Match each thing to the part of the plant that gave it.
pairs: the stem of the jute plant
the bark of the cinnamon tree
the white flesh inside a coconut
the fruit of the tamarind tree
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: People use almost every part of a plant: seeds, stems, fruits and wood. Knowing the part tells you how the plant must be grown and harvested.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Money plant, pepper, bitter gourd, pumpkin.
items.a: Pumpkin, because a pumpkin is a creeper that spreads along the ground. The others are climbers.
items.why: Money plant, pepper and bitter gourd grow upwards by holding on to a support. A pumpkin usually spreads on the soil. But if their tendrils find a fence, they will climb it, so the boxes are not perfectly neat.

items.p: In 1974, men came to cut down a forest near the village of Reni in the Himalayas. The trees had been sold for their wood. The women of the village hugged the trees to stop them. This was part of the Chipko movement.

views.who: Gaura Devi, who led the women of Reni
views.says: This forest gives us firewood, fodder for our animals and medicine. The roots hold the soil on our steep hillside. Without the trees, the hill will slide.

views.who: A carpenter in a city (an imagined view)
views.says: I need wood to make doors, tables and chairs. If no trees are ever cut, I have no work and families have no furniture.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Use what you know about how people use trees. Then say what the other side has right, and whether there could be a way to meet both needs.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For Gaura Devi: the forest gave the village food, fuel and medicine every day, and tree roots hold soil on slopes. For the carpenter: wood really is useful, and people need it. A strong answer then gives the other side its due, and may suggest a middle way, like planting trees to cut later and protecting forests on steep hills.
items.why: This was a real conflict between people who lived from the forest and people who wanted its wood. Both needs are real. Gaura Devi and the women of Reni saved their forest, and the movement led to new laws protecting Himalayan forests.

items.p: Draw the view from your window or balcony. Mark one tree, one shrub, one herb and one climber or creeper, if you can see them. Label how you knew each kind.
items.a: A drawing with plants labelled by kind, and a short clue for each, like 'one thick trunk' or 'soft green stem'.
items.why: Sorting real plants you can see is harder than sorting names. The labels show which stem clue you used.
items.context: In the Plant Count, you count the trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers and creepers you can see from home.

items.p: A friend says, 'Every plant with a green stem is a herb.' In the Stem Test, how could you find out if your friend is right?
items.a: Press a fingernail into the stem and bend it. A young stem from a tree can be green too, but it is firmer than a herb stem and turns woody with age. A green stem that does not dent and snaps when bent has wood in it, so it is not a herb.
items.why: A strong answer uses the tests from the experiment (dent, bend, stand) as evidence, not the colour alone.
items.context: In the Stem Test, you pressed, bent and held up pieces of stem to find out which were woody.

items.p: A climber needs less food to build a stem than a tree needs to build a trunk, so a climber can grow long quickly.
items.why: True. A thin stem costs little food, because a climber uses a tree, a wall or a stick to hold it up. A tree spends food on wood, year after year.

items.p: A coconut palm and a mango are both trees. Which is the coconut more closely related to?
items.why: Coconut palms belong to a big group of plants that also includes grasses like rice and bamboo. 'Tree' is a way of growing, not a family. Picking 'mango' means thinking trees must be cousins.

items.p: A tree trunk that is 2 metres around must be older than a trunk that is 1 metre around.
items.why: False. Different kinds of trees grow at different speeds. A fast tree in a wet, sunny place can grow fat quickly. A slow tree on a dry hill may take far longer. The rule of 2 and a half cm a year in Hug a Tree is only a rough guess.
items.context: In Hug a Tree, you measured around a tree trunk with string to guess the tree's age.

items.p: The hard material that makes wood strong, like a glue in the walls of its cells, is called ____.
items.why: Lignin and cellulose together make wood strong. Herbs have very little lignin, so their stems are soft.

items.p: The Great Banyan in the Botanic Garden at Howrah, near Kolkata, has thousands of prop roots that have become trunks. Their first trunk died and was removed in 1925. Scientists disagree about how to count them.

views.who: Scientists who count by genes and roots
views.says: All those trunks grew from one seed. They have the same genes and are joined together. So the Great Banyan is one plant.
Each trunk has their own roots and could live on alone if they were cut free. So each trunk is a separate plant.

items.ask: Is the Great Banyan one plant or thousands? Pick a side and give your reason. Then say what the other side has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For one plant: every trunk grew from the same seed, and they still share one body of branches. For many: each trunk can stand and feed themselves on their own. A strong answer then sees that the word 'one plant' was made for animals like us, and does not fit plants neatly.
items.why: This is still argued about. There is no single right answer. The puzzle shows that our ideas of 'one living thing' come from animals, and plants do not always fit them.

items.p: Tulsi starts with a soft stem and later grows a woody one. Is tulsi a herb or a shrub? Explain your answer.
items.a: Both, at different times. A young tulsi has a soft stem, so they are like a herb. An old tulsi has a woody stem, so they are a small shrub. The kinds are boxes we made, and some plants move between them.
items.why: Plants change as they grow. Our kinds are useful guides, not walls.

items.p: Many people think climbers are lazy, because they use other plants to hold them up. A climber still has hard work to do. Name two things a climber must do that a tree does not.
items.a: For example: a climber must find a support, so their tip circles slowly, searching. They must grab and hold on, with tendrils that coil, little roots that grip, or a stem that twists. They must also grow long very fast, to reach the light before other plants shade them.
items.why: A strong answer names real work, like searching, gripping or growing fast. Climbers do not build a trunk, but they spend their food and effort in other ways.

items.p: In a thick forest, very little light reaches the ground. Why might being a climber help a plant there? Why might being a climber be harder in an open field with no trees?
items.a: In a forest, a climber can use the tree trunks as supports and reach the light at the top, without building a trunk of their own. In an open field there is plenty of light, but nothing to climb, so the climber has to creep along the ground and may be trampled or shaded by grass.
items.why: A strong answer says a climber's way of growing works only when there is a support, and that the best kind of plant depends on the place.

items.p: In the Circling Shoot, a climber's tip moved in slow loops. Revathi, a girl in Class 4, says the wind did it. How could you test her idea?
opts: Keep the pot indoors with no fan or breeze, and see if it still circles
items.why: To test one idea, take away just that one thing. If the tip still circles with no wind, the plant is moving on their own. This is a fair test.
items.context: In the Circling Shoot, you photographed a climbing shoot's tip every 30 minutes to see if it moved.

items.p: Some herbs come from woody ancestors, and on some islands herbs have turned back into woody shrubs.
items.why: True. Plants have switched between woody and soft many times in their history. It is one reason 'tree' and 'herb' are not families.

items.p: A company makes a medicine from a plant that village healers have used for hundreds of years. Who do you think should get credit, and why?
items.a: Any thoughtful answer with a reason. For example, the healers should get credit, because they found the plant first. The scientists should too, because they tested it and made it safe. The village could share the money.
items.why: This is a real question. India and other countries have laws about sharing benefits from plants with the people who knew them first.

items.p: Put these in order of when they first appeared on Earth, oldest first: flowering plants, the first trees, the first tiny land plants.
items.why: Tiny land plants came first, about 470 million years ago. Trees came about 390 million years ago. Flowering plants came much later, more than 130 million years ago.

items.p: Aristotle said plants exist for the sake of animals and people. Do you agree? Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.a: Any answer with a reason each way. For: people use plants for almost everything. Against: plants lived for hundreds of millions of years before any people, and most plants are never used by people.
items.why: This is a debate, so there is no single right answer. A good answer gives reasons on both sides.

items.p: Draw a forest with a tree, a climber, a shrub and a creeper. Draw arrows to show how each one reaches the sunlight.
items.a: A tall tree reaching up, a climber climbing the tree, a shrub in a sunny gap and a creeper spreading in an open patch, each with an arrow to the sun.
items.why: All the kinds are different ways of reaching the same light.

items.p: About 390 million years ago, plants that could make wood began to grow much taller than all the others. Why did wood let them grow tall?
opts: Wood is stiff and strong, so a woody stem can hold leaves high up in the light
Wood is heavy, so the wind cannot move the plant
items.why: The lignin in wood makes the stem stiff. A stiff stem can stand tall and lift leaves above the plants around them, where they catch more light. Picking 'heavy' misses the point. Wood is strong for its weight, not just heavy.

items.p: Scientists think about 9,000 kinds of trees have not yet been found and named. Why might nobody have found them yet?
items.a: They may grow in places few botanists have visited, like remote hills and thick rainforest, or only at the very tops of tall trees. There are also far fewer botanists than there are places to search.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason about where trees grow and who looks for them.

quiz.p: You want to tell a tree, a shrub and a herb apart. Which part of the plant is the best clue?
quiz.why: The stem tells us most: one woody trunk for a tree, many woody stems for a shrub, a soft green stem for a herb. Picking flowers often means thinking all plants with flowers are alike.
Money plant holds on to a wall or pole with little roots and grows up it. Mango is a tree, rose is a shrub and spinach is a herb.
A watermelon plant spreads along the ground. Picking 'tulsi' often means thinking every small plant creeps. Tulsi stands up by themselves. Neem is a tree, and bamboo is a tall grass.

quiz.p: A climber has only a thin stem. How do they get their leaves up high?
opts: They hold on to a support and grow up it
quiz.why: A climber holds on to a tree, a wall or a stick, so they can reach the light with a thin stem. Picking 'they do not need light' is a common mistake. Climbers climb because they need light.

quiz.p: Which of these is made from a plant?
quiz.why: Paper is made from wood, which comes from tree trunks. Steel is made from iron in rocks, and glass is made from sand. Picking glass often means thinking anything see-through comes from leaves.

quiz.p: Why do towns plant big trees like neem along hot streets?
opts: Their shade and their leaves cool the street
Trees keep the street dark at night
quiz.why: The leaves block sunlight, and water evaporating from them cools the air. Shade is one of the most important ways people use trees. Picking 'make the road stronger' mixes up shade with roots.

quiz.p: In Shade Detective, why do we leave the thermometer for 3 minutes in each place before reading it?
opts: So it has time to warm up or cool down to that place
quiz.why: A thermometer takes a little time to reach the temperature around it. If you read it at once, it still shows the last place. Waiting the same time everywhere also keeps the test fair.
quiz.context: In Shade Detective, you measure how hot the ground is in the sun and in a tree's shade.

quiz.p: A papaya plant has one tall trunk, but the trunk is soft and spongy inside, with no hard wood. What is the best way to describe papaya?
opts: A plant that does not fit neatly into the five kinds
quiz.why: Papaya stands up like a tree, but their trunk is not woody like a tree's. So they sit between the boxes. The five kinds are a useful guide, but some plants do not fit them well.

quiz.p: Which of these is true about trees?
opts: All trees belong to one family
Plants from many different families became trees separately
Trees were the first plants on Earth
quiz.why: 'Tree' is a way of growing. Many unrelated families found it. Tiny land plants came long before trees.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not know?
opts: How many kinds of plants exist on Earth
quiz.why: More than 350,000 plant species are named, and about 2,000 new ones are named each year. Nobody knows the true total.

quiz.p: Many medicines first came from plants. Why must a new plant medicine be tested by scientists before people use it?
opts: Some plant chemicals are poisonous, and the safe amount must be found
Plants are always safe, so testing is only for fun
To make the medicine taste nice
quiz.why: The same plant can help in a small amount and harm in a large one. Kaner and datura are natural but very poisonous. Testing finds out what works and how much is safe. Picking 'always safe' is the mistake of thinking natural means harmless.

applications: Farmers choose kinds of plants by how they grow. Pepper and gourds need supports, pumpkins need space to creep.
Gardeners plant shrubs as hedges and climbers to cover walls and fences.
City planners plant trees along roads to shade people and cool the streets.
Carpenters choose woods like teak, sal and sheesham for strong furniture and doors.
Paper mills make paper from wood, bamboo and sugarcane waste.
Cloth is made from cotton, jute, linen from flax, and even banana fibre.
Rope and doormats are made from coir, the fibre from coconut husks.
Rubber for tyres and chappals comes partly from rubber trees grown in Kerala and the north-east.
Medicine makers test plants used by traditional healers to find new medicines.
Seed banks store seeds of many kinds of plants to protect them for the future.
Foresters measure trunks at chest height to work out how much wood a forest holds.
Botanists use the kinds of plants to describe forests, from tall rainforest to scrubby desert.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of plants are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: More than 350,000 are named, and about 2,000 new ones are named every year. Many places have never been properly explored.

open_questions.q: Is a clone like Pando or the Great Banyan one plant or many?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists disagree about what 'one individual' means for plants that share roots and genes.

open_questions.q: Do trees in a forest really share food through fungi, like a 'wood wide web'?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies found carbon moving between trees through fungi. Other scientists say the evidence is still weak. Research continues.

open_questions.q: Why did lignin, the hard glue in wood, appear when it did?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know roughly when wood appeared, but not exactly how plants first made lignin, or why so few living things can break it down.

open_questions.q: How old are the oldest trees in India?
open_questions.why_open: Many old tropical trees have no clear growth rings, so their ages are hard to measure. Scientists use other methods, which can give different answers.

open_questions.q: Which plants in India's forests hold medicines nobody has found yet?
open_questions.why_open: Only a small part of India's plants has been tested carefully. Many forests are being lost before they can be studied.

maths.problem: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, did a Plant Count from her windows. She counted 12 trees, 8 shrubs, 20 herbs, 4 climbers and 2 creepers. How many plants did she count in all? Which kind did she see most of?
maths.explain: Add them up: 12 + 8 is 20. 20 + 20 is 40. 40 + 4 is 44. 44 + 2 is 46. The biggest number is 20, for herbs, so she saw herbs most.
maths.context: This is about the Plant Count. You count plants of each kind with tally marks, looking from your windows and balcony.

chart.title: Lakshmi's Plant Count: plants of each kind

maths.why_maths: A tally and a bar chart turn a walk full of plants into numbers you can compare at a glance.

maths.problem: In Shade Detective, the sunny paving was 46 degrees and the ground under a big tree was 31 degrees. How many degrees cooler was the tree's shade?
maths.explain: Take the smaller number from the bigger one. 46 minus 31 is 15. Check: 31 + 15 is 46.
maths.context: This is about Shade Detective. You measured how hot the ground was in the sun and in a tree's shade with a thermometer.
maths.why_maths: Taking one temperature from the other tells us exactly how much a tree cools the ground, not just that the shade feels cooler.

maths.problem: In Hug a Tree, a neem trunk measured 150 cm around. Using the rough rule that many trees grow 2 and a half cm around each year, about how old are they?
maths.explain: Two lots of 2 and a half make 5. So every 5 cm around is about 2 years. 150 divided by 5 is 30. 30 lots of 2 years is 60 years. The tree is roughly 60 years old. Remember this is only a rough guess.
maths.context: This is about Hug a Tree. You measured around a trunk with string and used a rough rule to guess the tree's age.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by how much a tree grows each year turns a length into an age, so we can estimate something we cannot see.

maths.problem: Some bamboo can grow about 90 cm in one day. If they kept growing at that speed, how tall would a new shoot be after 4 days?
maths.answer: 360 cm, which is 3 metres and 60 centimetres.
maths.explain: 90 cm each day for 4 days is 4 groups of 90. 90 + 90 is 180. 180 + 180 is 360. So 360 cm. That is more than twice as tall as a grown-up.
maths.context: Bamboo is a giant grass, and some kinds grow very fast. This problem uses a real growing speed.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a growth speed by days shows how a grass can grow taller than a house in a few weeks.

maths.problem: In the Smell Test, three people scored tulsi 2, 5 and 4. What is the middle score?
maths.explain: Put the scores in order: 2, 4, 5. The middle one is 4. The middle score is fair, because one very high or very low score cannot pull it too far.
maths.context: This is about the Smell Test. Each person crushed and smelled leaves and scored the smell from 0 to 5.
maths.why_maths: Different noses give different scores. Ordering them and taking the middle gives one fair answer.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people learn to sort plants? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: About 2,300 years ago, a Greek thinker called Theophrastus wrote one of the first books about plants. He sorted plants by how they grow: trees, shrubs, undershrubs and herbs. For almost 2,000 years after that, many scholars sorted plants this way. Even in the 1680s, the English botanist John Ray split plants into trees and herbs first. Many people thought that all trees must be one natural group of relatives. Then botanists began comparing flowers, fruits and seeds instead of stems. In 1789, a French botanist, Antoine Laurent de Jussieu, grouped plants into families this way. His families mixed trees, shrubs and herbs together. The rose family holds the rose, a shrub, the apple, a tree, and the strawberry, a herb. From the 1990s, scientists compared plant genes, and found the same thing. Trees grew in many separate families, again and again.
how_we_found_out.who: Theophrastus, a Greek thinker; John Ray, an English botanist; Antoine Laurent de Jussieu, a French botanist
how_we_found_out.when: About 300 BCE (Theophrastus), the 1680s (Ray), 1789 (de Jussieu) and the 1990s (gene studies)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That all trees form one family of relatives. Comparing flowers and seeds, and later genes, showed that trees, shrubs and herbs are mixed together in the same families.
how_we_found_out.art: An old Greek scroll with drawings of a tree, a shrub and a herb, next to a rose, an apple and a strawberry joined by one family line.
